findings.claim: For the 4-mark Explain question, examiners want a chain of reasoning, not a list.
findings.truth: House rule: do not assert what examiners want. State the technique directly.
findings.evidence: checker brief: fabricated examiner claims are a fix

findings.claim: The 3 SPaG marks per paper reward precise terms
findings.truth: Paper 1 carries up to 4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar and specialist terminology. Every other lesson in the unit says 4.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview (94 marks, up to 4 SPaG) and the Topic 1 assessment information section

findings.claim: Examine how global atmospheric circulation influences the location of biomes around the world. (8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
findings.truth: Biome distribution is Topic 7 content, examined on Paper 3. Paper 1 sets the location of arid (high pressure) and high rainfall (low pressure) areas.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1b; the Paper 1 content overview lists Topics 1-3 only

findings.claim: examiners want CO2 ppm rises, named feedback loops, named places affected
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1: give the instruction without attributing it to examiners.

findings.claim: Hurricane Katrina's 8.5 m surge in 2005 destroyed New Orleans levees
findings.truth: The peak surge, about 8.2 m (27 ft), struck the Mississippi coast. The New Orleans surge was about 4.3 m, and that is what broke the levees.

findings.claim: Examiners want named cases, specific death tolls, specific dollar costs
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1. Also British English: costs, not dollar costs.

findings.claim: deaths often kept low (Sandy ~233 in USA)
findings.truth: Hurricane Sandy killed 254 people across the USA, the Caribbean and Canada. US deaths were about 160 (71 direct, 87 indirect, 2 offshore).

findings.claim: A magnitude 6.9 quake in Christchurch, New Zealand (2011) killed 185.
findings.truth: The February 2011 Christchurch earthquake was magnitude 6.3. The death toll of 185 is right. The 6.9 figure looks like a blend with the 7.1 Darfield quake of September 2010.

findings.claim: Examiners reward primary vs secondary impact distinctions
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: Fertility rate (births per woman) is around 1.6 in the UK and 4.5 in Niger
findings.truth: Niger has the highest fertility rate in the world, about 6 children per woman. The UK rate is about 1.4. A flashcard repeats the 4.5 figure and calls it 'among the highest in the world'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Demographics of Niger (6.06, 2023); Wikipedia, Total fertility rate (UK 1.39, 2025)

findings.claim: It combines three measures: GDP per capita (income), mean and expected years of schooling (education), and life expectancy (health).
findings.truth: The HDI has used GNI per capita for the income dimension since the 2010 report, not GDP per capita.

findings.claim: Examiners reward students who pair GDP with Gini in their answers.
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: examiners reward students who balance top-down AND bottom-up examples
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: Three Gorges cost over $40 bn, much from World Bank loans creating debt
findings.truth: The World Bank refused to finance the Three Gorges Dam on environmental and resettlement grounds. It was paid for domestically, through Chinese state banks, bonds and power revenue, with some export credits.

findings.claim: India's rapid <dfn ...>core-periphery inequality</dfn> growth has changed its position in the world.
findings.truth: The definition tag was dropped into the middle of the sentence, so the sentence now says nothing. The tag and its data-def are kept; the sentence is repaired around them.

findings.claim: around 230 million still live on under $3.65 a day
findings.truth: 230 million is the UN multidimensional poverty count for India (228.9 million), from the same report as the 415 million figure in the previous sentence. It is not an income threshold; far more than 230 million Indians live under $3.65 a day.

findings.claim: examiners reward depth over breadth
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: rapid expansion of solar power (160 GW capacity 2024)
findings.truth: India had about 82 GW of installed solar in March 2024 and about 97 GW by December 2024. It passed 160 GW in 2026.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Solar power in India (81,813 MW at 31 Mar 2024; 164.59 GW July 2026)

findings.claim: Examiner tip: always show the working, even if the final figure is wrong - method marks are awarded.
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1: do not assert how a board's mark scheme allocates marks.

findings.claim: For a 12-mark megacity case-study question, examiners expect specific named places
findings.truth: Paper 1 has no 12-mark question. The longest item is 8-mark extended writing, with up to 4 SPaG marks on the paper.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview and Topic 3 assessment information

findings.claim: mark schemes reward specifics
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: Mumbai is now India's busiest container port and home to its largest international airport.
findings.truth: Delhi's Indira Gandhi International is India's largest airport. Mumbai's is the second busiest.
findings.evidence: AAI passenger traffic data; Wikipedia airport articles

findings.claim: connectivity includes 1,400 km of suburban rail
findings.truth: The Mumbai Suburban Railway network is about 450 km (585.9 km including the Vasai-Roha line). It is still the world's busiest commuter system, so that part stands.

findings.claim: especially from the poorer states of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Maharashtra
findings.truth: Maharashtra is India's richest large state and is Mumbai's own state. Migrants do come from its rural districts, but it is not a poorer state.

findings.claim: Examiners expect named projects (Mumbai Metro, SPARC toilets)
findings.truth: Same house rule as F1.

findings.claim: India is the world's fifth-largest economy (repeated in the key fact, the conclusion and knowledge check [2], which keys 'fifth')
findings.truth: The nominal-GDP rank is volatile. The current IMF table used by Wikipedia puts India 6th for 2026 ($4.15 tn), behind Japan and the UK, while the April 2025 IMF projections were widely reported as putting India 4th ahead of Japan. Options: (a) leave it, and accept it will be wrong in one direction or the other; (b) drop the volatile rank from the prose ('one of the world's five or six largest economies') and re-key the knowledge check onto the stable fact that India is 3rd by purchasing power, which the same key fact already states. Recommend (b).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, List of countries by GDP (nominal), IMF 2026 estimates
findings.ruling: Leave: needs a source check or a ripple through keyed answers (relabel queue).

findings.claim: Hurricane Katrina caused 1,800 deaths (content_html, and the stem plus answer key of the 4-mark calculation: 138,000 / 1,800 = 76.67)
findings.truth: The National Hurricane Center cut Katrina's official toll from 1,833 to 1,392 in January 2023. Most GCSE textbooks still print 1,800. Adopting 1,392 means re-keying the calculation to 138,000 / 1,392 = 99.1 (accept 99-100) and editing both the stem and the mark scheme. Recommend adopting 1,392 and re-keying, since the question supplies its own figures and nothing else depends on 1,800.
findings.ruling: Leave: needs a source check or a ripple through keyed answers (relabel queue).

findings.claim: The atmosphere does about half of the global heat transfer. The other half is done by ocean currents.
findings.truth: Research puts the atmosphere well above half of poleward heat transport at most latitudes. GCSE textbooks vary, so the split is not settled enough to correct surgically.
findings.evidence: Trenberth and Caron (2001) heat transport estimates

findings.claim: The Coriolis effect deflects rising Ferrel-cell air, producing south-westerly prevailing winds.
findings.truth: Prevailing winds are surface winds. The deflected air is the poleward surface flow of the Ferrel cell, not rising air. The content_html gets this right.

findings.claim: Arctic sea-ice extent has declined by about 13% per decade; IPCC projects 1.5C to 4.4C by 2100
findings.truth: 13% per decade is the September minimum, not the annual mean (about 3-4% per decade). The IPCC AR6 lower best estimate is 1.4C (SSP1-1.9), not 1.5C. Neither would cost a mark.
findings.evidence: NSIDC/NASA sea-ice trends; IPCC AR6 WG1 SPM

findings.claim: The World Bank classifies countries as low income (under $1,135 per year) ... high income (over $13,845)
findings.truth: Those bands are set by GNI per capita, not GDP per capita, and are revised every July. The values quoted match the FY2024 thresholds.
findings.evidence: World Bank country classifications by income level

findings.claim: Norway typically tops the index (0.96); Cuba has GDP per capita roughly a tenth of the UK's
findings.truth: Switzerland and Iceland have led recent HDI reports; Norway's value is about 0.97. Cuban GDP per capita in US dollars is not a settled figure after the 2021 peso devaluation, and the pre-2021 ratio to the UK was nearer a quarter.
findings.evidence: UNDP HDR 2023-24 and 2025; World Bank Cuba series

findings.claim: fertility rate fallen from 5.4 in 1960; over 22 official languages; It now leads the Quad security partnership
findings.truth: The World Bank series gives India about 5.9 in 1960. The Eighth Schedule lists exactly 22 scheduled languages, so 'over 22' overshoots. India is a member of the Quad, not its leader. None is mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: World Bank fertility series; Constitution of India, Eighth Schedule

findings.claim: Traffic congestion costs the city an estimated 8% of GDP a year; property prices the same as central London; around half of Mumbai's residents live in informal housing (41% elsewhere in the lesson)
findings.truth: The congestion figure traces to no settled source (published estimates are nearer 2-3% of city GDP). Central London prime prices are well above Mumbai's in absolute terms. 'Around half' and '41% in slums' can both be true if informal housing is read more widely than census slums, but the two figures sit oddly together in one lesson.

findings.claim: Deonar methane-capture plant generating 12 MW; 1,800 BEST diesel buses switched to electric; around 250,000 ragpickers in Mumbai
findings.truth: None could be confirmed from a settled published source within the fetch budget. Reported Deonar waste-to-energy capacity is lower, BEST's electric fleet was around 1,000 buses in 2024-25, and Mumbai waste-picker counts published elsewhere are far below 250,000. Worth a check before these numbers are quoted in a demo.

summary: 25 fixes across all 10 lessons: three exam-claim errors (Paper 1 has 4 SPaG marks not 3, and no 12-mark question), one wrong earthquake magnitude, Niger's fertility rate, the HDI income measure, the Katrina surge location, Sandy's US death toll, the Three Gorges funding claim, Mumbai's rail length and airport claim, India's solar capacity and poverty measure, a garbled definition sentence, and a ten-lesson sweep of unverifiable 'examiners want/reward' claims. Two ADJUDICATE items: India's volatile GDP rank (also keyed in a knowledge check) and the revised Katrina death toll, which is used inside a calculation answer key. All knowledge check keys, match orders and every calculation in the unit recompute correctly.
